newsitem.title: UK: British doctors warn of tuna food poisoning risk.
newsitem.headline: British doctors warn of tuna food poisoning risk.

text.p: Food poisoning from tuna fish could be more common than believed, British doctors said on Wednesday.
Emergency specialist Ian Stell at Guy's Hospital in London said about 50 cases of scombrotoxin poisoning were reported each year in the Britain, but the condition could be under-diagnosed.

"It may be that many episodes are ascribed to food sensitivity, and the reported numbers may not reflect the true incidence of this condition," Stell wrote in a report in the Journal of Accident and Emergency Medicine.
Stell and colleagues described the cases of two men who contracted scombrotoxin poisoning an hour after eating tuna.
One 45-year-old man was poisoned by eating freshly cooked tuna in a wine bar. The other, 31, was poisoned by a tuna-mayonnaise sandwich.
The condition causes a swollen throat, flushes, rashes, headaches and diarrhoea.
"Scombrotoxin poisoning should be considered in any patient who suffers the typical symptoms after eating fish," Stell wrote.
Tuna and mackerel are the most common causes but it has also been passed on by herrings, pilchards, sardines and anchovies.
Affected fish may look and smell all right, but often it has a hot or peppery taste. Victims usually recover within a day and antihistamines help the symptoms.
